The appellant, who was the sole executor of the will, died in July, 1903 leaving behind his adopted son, the appellant, and two daughters, Gundamma, who were the sons of the appellant. The appellant 's adopted son, Gundayya, was married to the appellant on August 22, 1945, and the appellant had a son, G. Kalbagal, who died in December, 1908. The appellant was married to one G. Parthasarathy lyengar, who died on January 14, 1944, and the two daughters, K.V. Sivaraman and K.V, who were their sons, were daughters of Gundamma. The appellant made a gift of properties, items 1 and 2, in favour of Gundayya and the properties were bequeathed to him. The appellant claimed a decree for possession against Gundamma and a further prayer for the payment of current mesne profits by respondent 1. The trial court dismissed the suit. The High Court, in appeal, held that the appellant was entitled to the properties in question, and that the appellant had no right to the properties. The High court also held that the will was not proved by the appellant. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the High Court was not justified in reversing the finding of the trial court on the question of the due and valid execution of the will. Held, that the High court was not justified to reverse the finding of fact of the trial Court on the question about the due and lawful execution of the wills, and that, in recording the findings of the trial Judge on the question, the High Court had not fully or properly considered all the relevant evidence. The High Courts were not justified in recording the conclusions of the trial judge on the question regarding the validity of the will and the subsisting title of the testatrix in respect of all the properties covered by the will. The High courts were not justified to interfere with the findings of fact of courts below on the question whether the will was proved by the appellants.

The appellant, a trustee of a temple, was elected as a trustee by the Sengunatha Amma of Manjakollai village. The appellant was elected as the trustee by the respondent. The respondent took a different view and proceeded on the basis that trusteeship of the temple was not hereditary. The Subordinate Judge held that the appellant was a hereditary trustee and the suit was not barred by limitation. The High Court in appeal reversed the decision of the Subordinate Judge. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The appellant was a trustee within the meaning of section 6(9) of the Madras Act 19 of 1951. The expression "regulated by usage" in section 6(10) of the Act must be construed along with the phrase "succession to this office" and when so construed that part of the definition would only apply where the ordinary rules of succession under the Hindu law are modified by usage and succession has to be determined in accordance with the modified rules. [446 E F] (ii) The expression "successions to this office " in section 6 (9) of Madras Act 19 Of 1951 must be construed in the light of the phrase "for a fixed period of one year and not for life. It is not possible to say that there is a succession of As office to another when on the expiration of the period for which a person was appointed, there is a vacancy and B is elected to that vacancy. [447 E F]

The petitioners were working in various offices in the State of Andhra Pradesh. The Government of Andhra Pradesh, by an order dated January 21, 1969, relieved them of service. The posts so rendered vacant were filled by qualified candidates possessing domicile qualifications and in cases where such candidates were not available the posts were left unfilled till qualified domicile candidates become available. The posts were to be filled by qualified persons possessing domicile qualifications. The Government passed an order on January 21,1969 relieving before February 28, 1969 all non domicile persons appointed on or after November 1, 1956 to certain categories of posts reserved for domiciles of Telengana region. The Government by its order dated January 28, 1969 relieved before February 28 1969 all non- domicile persons appointed in the Andhra region to certain categories. The petitioners were not eligible for appointment to the posts reserved for close quarters. The Government issued a notification on January 21 1969 relieving before February 27, 1969 all Non domicile persons appointed by or on or after the date of the said order. The petitioners challenged the validity of the said notification on the grounds that the said notification was ultra vires the Constitution. The petitioners contended that the notification was ultra. tO the Constitution and that the notification violated the guarantee of equality enshrined in article 14 of the Constitution. Dismissing the petitions, HELD: (1) The notification was not ultra vires the constitution. The notification was issued in exercise of the power conferred by section 3 of the Andhra Pradesh Public Employment (Requirement as to Residence) Act, 1957. The notification did not contravene the provisions of article 14 of Constitution. [118G] (2) The notification is not ultra vires. The notification is ultra vires the Presidential Order. [118C] (3) The notification issued by the Government was not in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution and the notification was not in conformity with the provisions contained in the Constitution. [119D] (4) The notification cannot be said to be in violation of the provisions of Article 14 of the constitution. [119E] (5) The notification dated January 21 1969 was not in compliance with the provisions in the Constitution and was not in violation of article 14. [119F] (6) The notification did in fact violate the provisions of articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution as it was not in consonance with the provisions. [119G] (7) The notification does not contravene the fundamental rights guaranteed under article 14 of our Constitution. [120F] (8) The notification contravenes the provisions of Articles 14 and 16. The appellant was convicted under section 52 of the Indian Post Office Act, 1898, and sentenced to one year 's rigorous imprisonment. The High Court confirmed his acquittal. The appellant appealed to this Court by special leave. The appellant contended that the search was illegal inasmuch as the appellant had in his possession the key of which was produced by him. Held, that the search in question was illegal inasmuch that the appellant had the opportunity to get the articles and that the search could be resisted by the person whose premises were sought to be searched. The search was illegal. The search could be challenged only by the person who was in the possession of the key and not by the appellant. The search in question had not been proved. The appellant had no opportunity to get it. The search had not been established. The search having not been proved, the conviction could not be sustained.

The appellant was charged with the offence of murder. The prosecution case was that on the night between June 14, 1960, he was in the field of one Paley Singh and that on the morning of June 14, he was having a bath there. The appellant was taken in custody and was taken in the lock up. The Sub Inspector took his thumb impression forcibly on three papers, but did not tell him the reason. The appellant adduced no evidence in support of his statement. The Courts below rightly did not accept his version. The evidence led by the prosecution consisted of the evidence relating to motive, to his extra judicial confession to one Paleya, and the evidence led by him consisted of the testimony relating to motive. The High Court did not rely on this extra judicial confession. It relied on certain statements made by the appellant in his report, and considered those facts together with the motive and the evidence about the purchase of the sword by the appellant. The High court did not rely upon this extra judicial confessional statement. The High ' Court did not consider the evidence of Paley. The High, Court did not accept the version of the appellant regarding the appellant 's extra judicial confession and that the extra judicial confession together with the circumstances relied on by the High Court, fully made out the prosecution case against the appellant. Held, that the extrajudicial confession of the appellant to the Police Officer was inadmissible in evidence as it was not corroborated by the evidence of the appellant. It was not proved that the appellant had murdered Sheo Sahai. The extra judicial confession of the appel lant was not corroborated. The extrajudicial confession was not corroborated in material particulars by the evidence led in support of the prosecution case. The extra Judicial confession was not proved to be true. The extra-judicial confession was inadmissible in the evidence as it related to the appellant.

The respondent was tried by the Special Court for an offence under section 5(1) of the West Bengal Special Courts Ordinance, 1949, which was replaced in March, 1950, by the West Bengal Act X of 1950. The Special Court convicted him and sentenced him to various terms of imprisonment. The respondent appealed to the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court held that the Special Court had no jurisdiction to try the case inasmuch as section 5(2) of the Act was not applicable to the case and that the Special Courts Act was not saved by article 14 of the Constitution and that the special court had no jurisdiction in the case. The High court further held that the special Court had no power to try the respondent under article 13(2) as it was not a court of appeal and that the High Court had no inherent jurisdiction to quash the conviction and sentence. The State of West Bengal appealed to this Court. Held, that the High court was in error in holding that the Special court had no inherent power to try a case. The special court had jurisdiction to try a particular case and the High Court was in error. The special Court had jurisdiction to entertain a case and the special court was not a Court of appeal and the High court had no power under article 226 to quash the order of conviction and sentence passed by the Special court. The special courts Act was not a law within the meaning of article 13(1) and was not saved from the provisions of article 14. The special Courts Act was a special law and the special courts Act had no application to the case.

The first and the main point argued before this Court was that the Tribunal after holding that there was no comparable industry in the region comparable with the Company came to the view that there were other industries in the region in which minimum wages were higher than the minimum wages paid by the company, and, therefore, the Tribunal committed an error in fixing the minimum wages which should be paid on an entirely different basis. HELD : The Tribunal committed an erroneous error in fixing minimum wages at the rate of three months ' basic wage in each case and in holding that there were only two other industries in that region in which the minimum wages were less than the minimum wage paid by the Company. The Tribunal committed no error of law in fixing the wage structure for these two industries. The Tribunal was not justified in fixing the wages of the workmen at the rate fixed by the Tribunal. [665 A] The Tribunal had not applied the principle of industry cum region. The appellant was a firm carrying on business in partnership with a limited company. The firm was dissolved and the appellant was assessed to income tax for the years 1948 49 and 1949 50. The claim was rejected by the Income tax Officer and by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Income tax Appellate Tribunal on appeal to the High Court. The High Court held that the appellant was not entitled to any relief under section, 25(4). The appellant came to this Court by special leave. Held, that the appellant had not been able to satisfy the High Court that the business of the firm was not liable to tax under section 25 (4) of Income tax Act. The business of the appellant was a business carried on by a firm which was dissolved and was assessed to tax under the Income tax, Act, 1922. The business was not a business of a firm which had been discontinued and the business was not discontinued. The business had not been discontinued and there was no succession to the business. The business must be regarded as one carried on by the firm and the appellant must be regarded to be a firm. The plaintiffs ' land was leased out to the respondents in respect of a lease of 96 bighas out of the land in dispute. The respondents claimed that the lease was not transferable and that the lease had been granted to them by the Inspector of Mines. The respondents denied that they had encroached upon the land and stated that the lease deed was not a lease deed. The trial court held that the lease in favour of the respondents was not transferable, that the lease did not create a lease and that the respondents had no right to the land and that the appellant had no right of renewal of the lease. The High Court dismissed the appeal. The appellant contended that the lease could not be said to be transferable and that it was not transferable. Held, that the respondents were not entitled to the benefit of the rule. The lease was not a transfer of a right to enjoy the land and the appellant was not entitled to any relief. The lease in favour the respondents was a lease of a permanent right and the appellant had a right to the lease. It was not a right to renewal of the lessee 's lease. The lease had been created by the Inspector and the respondents had a right of renewal. The lease did not confer a right of extension of the lease but only a right to a renewal. The right of renewal was not a mere right to renewal. The grant of a lease was not transfer of a lease. The grant was not a permanent right. The grant had been made by the Inspector in accordance with the rules and regulations of the Government. The grant could not be a permanent right, but a renewal of the right was a permanent right which was not transferable but a renewal.

The suit was dismissed by the Trial Court. The respondent filed an appeal to the High Court. The High Court held that the suit was not maintainable as the appellant had not been given an opportunity to lead evidence and that the suit had been decided in favour of the respondent. The High. Court also held that the appellant was not entitled to lead evidence. The High, Court also held, that the appellant had been given an adequate opportunity to lead the evidence and to lead evidence in support of the case. The High ' Court also held the appellant was entitled to lead additional evidence. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The High Court had no jurisdiction to record a finding on the issue of res judicata in a revision application filed against an order refusing to uphold an objection to certain question asked to a witness under examination. The expression "case" is not limited in its import to the entirety of the matter in dispute in an action. The expression 'case ' is not limited to the entirety. To interpret the expression "case", as an entire proceeding only and not a part of the proceeding imposes an unwarranted restriction on the exercise of powers of superintendence and may result in certain cases in denying relief to the aggrieved litigant where it is most needed and may result, in the perpetration of gross injustice. [439 D, G H] (ii) The expression "suit" is not restricted in its import. It includes a civil proceeding and is not restricted by anything contained in section 115 of the Code to the entirety, of the proceeding in a civil court. [440 D] Major section section Khanna vs Brig. F. J. Dillon, ; , referred to. (iii) The expression 'suit ' is not restricted to the entire proceeding only, and not a Part of the proceeding. [441 D] Major Section section Khanna vs S. D. Dillon [1963] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 887, referred to.

The appellants were employed as a bus conductor and the respondent was dismissed from service. The appellants filed a complaint under section 33 of the (XIV of 1947) read with section 33(1) of the ( XIV of 1947) against the appellants and their workmen alleging that the conciliation proceedings had been terminated for a period of more than 14 days. The appellants contended that the conciliation proceeding was not pending when the conciliation proceedings were taken and the appellants were not liable to be convicted under section 31(1) read with s. 33(1). Held, that the conciliation, proceedings were not pending when Louis Pereira was dismissed. The conciliation proceedings were not terminated when the conciliation proceeding is over and the conciliation proceedings are not terminated when there is no settlement. The conciliation proceeding was terminated for a reasonable cause and the appellants could not be convicted under s. 31(1). The termination of the conciliation proceedings was not a valid discharge of the appellants ' liability under section 31 of the Act. The termination of conciliation proceedings was a discharge of the duties of the bus conductor and was not a discharge of a workman. The termination was a discharge simpliciter of the appellants and was not an act of a workman within the meaning of section 31(2)(b) of the Act, and the termination was not a dismissal of the appellants. The termination could not be said to be a discharge of an employee. The termination did not terminate when the conciliation was over and the appellants ' dismissal was not a punishment. The termination, therefore, was a discharge. The termination in the present case was a discharge for a reasonable reason and the termination could not therefore be said to have been a discharge of service. The termination being a discharge simpliciter, the termination was a dismissal. The termination having been made for a reasonable or valid reason, the termination could be said to take place when the conciliation officer is required under section 12(6) of the .

The appellants claimed that the properties were granted to the predecessor of the appellants, and their predecessors were the trustees, and that they were entitled to the possession of the properties. The trial Judge found that the grant of the Inam was a personal Inam and that it was not a grant in favour of the appellants within the meaning of the Act. He further held that the appellants had proved their title to the suit properties. The lower appellate Court held that the alienor must be deemed to have resigned his office or left it. The lower Appellate Court held that it was necessary to consider the question whether the grant was in favour of a religious endowment within the meaning Of the Act. The High Court, however, held that the transfer of the properties was a personal inam and that it could not be said that the alienee had been removed from the management of the temple. The appellants appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The appellants had proved the title of the appellants to the suit property. The appellants had been removed by respondent No. 4, and they had been removed. The appellants were not holding the same as managers of the temple, and the transfer was a personal endowment. The appellants could not be deemed to be the trustees of the temple and the transfer could not be held to be a personal inam. [123 D E] (ii) The appellants were entitled to possession of the suit properties by virtue of the provisions of the Act, and the appellants were entitled only to the possession thereof. [123 G] (iii) The appellants ' suit was not barred by article 134 B of the Act because the transfer of properties was a family endowment. [123 F]

The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. The appellants appealed to this Court by certificate granted by the High Court. Held, that the provisions of section 14 of the Act are not void to the extent they prohibit persons whose names did not have a market. The appellants contended that the High Court had no power to enhance the sentence and that the High ' Court had no jurisdiction to enhance the death sentence. Held, that the High court had no power under section 377 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to enhance the capital sentence. The High court had the power to enhance it if it thought fit to do so. The High ' Court was not invested with the power to alter the capital sentence but was invested with the powers of the High Court to enhance the same. The assessee was assessed to income tax for the years 1943 44 to 1947 1948 and 1951 1952 by the Third Income tax Officer, C.I.T., Bombay, at and for Rs. 40,178 4 0. The Income tax Officer issued a notice of demand on the assessee for payment of tax. The assessee did not appear in person on the appointed day but on the next day the 17th June 1955, an Advocate acting on behalf of the assessee wrote a letter to the Additional Collector purporting to show cause why he should not be apprehended and confined to civil jail in satisfaction of the said certified demand. The sale proclamation was issued on the 25th February 1955, and the sale was held on the 25 th February 1955 fetching a price of Rs. 33,000 and it was confirmed on the 30th March 1955. The sale proceeds not being sufficient to satisfy the assessed tax the Additional Collector on the 7th June 1955 issued a warrant of arrest under section 13 of the Bombay City Land Revenue Act, 1876. The assessee was actually arrested on the 1st July 1955. On the 8th July 1955 an application was made by the present petitioner to the Bombay High Court under article 226 of the Constitution for the relief of the writ of habeas corpus for the production and release of the assessee. The High Court dismissed the petition. The present appeal is by special leave granted by this Court. Held, that the application must be dismissed. The rule of the Court is that the person who is arrested must be informed of the grounds on which the arrest is made and must be given an opportunity to make a representation against the arrest. The rule is not a rule of law but a rule of practice and is not a sound rule. The rule must be reasonable and must not be arbitrary. The rule has to be reasonable and not arbitrary. The law as it now stands can be supported on the grounds mentioned by the Court and the law as it then stood can be supported by a clear and cogent ground. The Court must be satisfied that the person arrested is not guilty of any offence and that he is not likely to commit any offence. The rule should be reasonable and should not be arbitrary, vague and fanciful.

The appellants were the workmen of the Bombay Port Trust. The respondents to the appeal were the trustees of the Port Trust. They were represented by the Bombay Port Workers ' Union. The Trustees, by a letter dated June 30, 1953, made a demand for a fixed recess of two hours. The Trustees sought to have the system of work of the Port of Bombay introduced by the Government of India Act, 1935, a new shift system of work in the Port Trust, but the Port Trust refused to do so. The respondents thereupon filed a reference under section 10(2) of the Act before the Central Government Industrial Tribunal, Bombay, which held that the Union was not able to establish that the existing system of work needed any modification. The Tribunal held that the respondents were not able to prove that the existing scheme of work required any modification. On appeal by the respondents, the Tribunal held that there was no evidence to show that the existing practice was not followed by the Port Trust and that the respondents had not been able to establish the existing system. The Tribunal also held that the Port Trust had not been given a reasonable opportunity to show that there was any justification for the change of the system of working. The respondents appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The Tribunal was right in holding that the respondents ' case was not established. The respondents were not entitled to any relief. [617 B] (ii) The Tribunal had not been shown to have been able to prove the existing system and the respondents had been able to show that they were entitled to be paid the normal wages for the period of rest of the period of the work. [618 B] (iii) The Tribunal has not been able in law to prove that there was a change in the system of the Port Trusts. The Tribunal has also not been able, to prove that it was not possible to establish the new system of work. [718 C]

The appellant instituted a suit for ejectment of three persons from the property in suit. The respondent contended that the suit was bad for non joinder of parties. The trial court decreed the suit. On appeal the Subordinate Judge held that the appellant was not entitled to the benefit of the Calcutta Thika Tenancy Act, 1949 as he was a thika tenant. The High Court in second appeal reversed the decision of the Subordinate Judge and held that the suit must be dismissed. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The Act of 1949 was a temporary measure and the landlord had to establish his right as a thika tenant in view of the provisions of section 3 of the Act. The Act of 1948 was a temporary Act and the landlord could not have established his rights in the absence of any grounds. The Act was a temporary one and the landlord was entitled to evict the tenant. [175 E F] (ii) The Act was not retrospective in operation. The Act had to be read as a temporary measure. The Act did not make any provision for transfer of pending suits. The Act, therefore, was not retrospective. The Act could not be said to be retrospective in operation and the landlord must be deemed to have established his right as such. [175 F G] (iii) The Act did no affect pending suits and appeals. The Act as finally amended could not apply to pending suits and appealable tenants. The Act would be applicable to pending suits. [175 G]

The appellant, who was the owner of a large tract of land, granted a lease for a period of 20 years to the respondent, who was a minor, for a period not exceeding one year. The respondent 's application for renewal of the lease was rejected by the appellant. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the appellant. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Government had no power to terminate the lease without giving any notice to the appellant, and that the Government was not bound to renew the lease without assigning any reasons. Held, that the Government must do something to avoid them, and there was no warrant for saying that the avoidance must be under the terms of the third proviso to section 20(1) of the Abolition Act. The second proviso to section. 20(1), which was introduced by the Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) (Amendment) Act, 1956, provides that the period of lease shall be one year from the date of the lease, and the lessee shall be entitled to renewal of the said lease for a further period of one year. It is not necessary that the lessee should have been given a notice of termination of the lease. The Government must do what it should have done in the instant case. The Government should have allowed the application for renewal, and the Government should have granted the lease under r. 47 of the Mineral Concession Rules of 1949.
